summary: The day's numpy mechanics (a dense layer's forward pass, a valid unflipped kernel slide, a bag-of-words row) rebuild in a few lines of plain Python with lists, and its judgements (classical or deep, which network type, when a CNN earns its place, transform against fit_transform) fit choice tasks; nothing can run numpy, scipy or scikit-learn in the page, so no task touches those libraries.

steps.title: Deep learning: models that learn their own features
steps.reason: The step has no behaviour a check can see without scikit-learn, but it teaches a judgement the reader can get wrong: a small table, or a decision that must be explained, still suits a classical model. The page names the wrong ways (expecting a deep network to win on any data, expecting its weights to explain a decision), so it fits a choice task.

steps.title: Types of neural networks
steps.reason: No Python behaviour, but the step teaches a method the reader applies: ask what one input looks like and pick the architecture that reads that shape. A scenario question tests that judgement rather than recall of a name, and the page names why each wrong pick fails (a feedforward network flattens away neighbours, a recurrent one reads sequences, an autoencoder is for unlabelled data).

steps.title: An artificial neural network: neurons, layers and a forward pass
steps.reason: A dense layer's forward pass is a return value: weighted sum, plus bias, through ReLU, with weights stored as (inputs, units). It rebuilds in plain Python with nested lists and loops, and the page's mistakes (reading the matrix the wrong way round, dropping the bias, skipping the activation) each give different numbers. ReLU stays at its one line, inside the anti-spoiler row.

steps.title: How a CNN reads an image: kernels, convolution and pooling
steps.reason: Sliding a kernel over a grid with mode "valid" is a returned grid a check can compare, written in plain Python with lists since scipy is not in the runtime. The page's two mistakes, flipping the kernel as convolve2d does and getting the n - k + 1 output size wrong, both show up in the result.

steps.title: Image classification: pixels, a baseline and what a CNN adds
steps.reason: The step's point is a judgement, not a computation: a CNN earns its place on large images where objects move, while the flat baseline already scores 96 percent on small centred digits. Its only computable pieces (flattening row by row, the inputs-times-units count) have no wrong answer beyond not writing them, so it fits a choice task on the page's named trade-offs.

steps.title: NLP techniques: tokens, bag of words, TF-IDF and n-grams
steps.reason: A bag-of-words row over a given vocabulary is a returned list of counts, built with lower(), split() and a loop. The page names what a check can catch: case folding, repeated words counted, words outside the vocabulary silently dropped, and word order ignored so two reordered titles give the same row. TF-IDF and n-grams stay on the page, since one task per step keeps to counting.

steps.title: NLP components and applications: routing ticket titles
steps.reason: The pipeline runs on scikit-learn, which the runtime does not have, and a plain-Python vectorizer would repeat step 5. The step teaches a judgement the page and the brief name as a pitfall: a new title goes through the training vocabulary with transform or the pipeline's predict, never fit_transform, so it fits a choice task.

tasks.title: Deep learning
tasks.idea: A lender has 4,000 rows of application-form columns and must tell every refused applicant why the model said no. The right pick is a classical model such as logistic regression or a tree, because the columns are already chosen, the table is small and each decision has to be explained.
checks: Picking a deep network because it learns its own features catches the belief that deep learning always wins; the page says it needs large labelled datasets and the features here are already chosen columns.
Picking a deep network because its weights can be read to explain each refusal catches the belief that a network is interpretable; the page says its thousands of weights are hard to read.

Picking a deep network because 4,000 rows is plenty catches the misreading of the data needs; the page says hundreds to thousands of rows can be enough for a classical model, while a deep network needs large labelled datasets.
tasks.q: A lender has 4,000 rows of application-form columns, such as income and loan amount, and must tell every refused applicant why the model said no. Which model do you pick?
options: It learns its own features from the columns, so a deep network.
Its weights can be read to explain each refusal, so a deep network.
The table is small and refusals need reasons, so a classical model.
4,000 labelled rows is plenty of data, so a deep network.
tasks.explain: The columns are already chosen, hundreds to thousands of rows can be enough for a classical model, and its coefficients or tree splits can be read to explain each refusal. A deep network pays off when it learns its own features from raw pixels or words on large labelled datasets, and its thousands of weights are hard to read.

tasks.title: Types of neural networks
tasks.idea: A factory has thousands of labelled photos from a production line, each marked defective or not, and wants a network to flag defects. The right pick is a convolutional network, because one input is an image and a CNN reads grid data with the same detector at every position.
checks: Picking a feedforward network on the flattened pixels catches the idea that any input can be a table row; the page says flattening loses the fact that two pixels were neighbours.
Picking a recurrent network such as an LSTM catches choosing by popularity rather than input shape; the page says it reads a sequence in order, and a photo is not one.
Picking an autoencoder catches missing what the labels mean; the page says an autoencoder suits unlabelled data you want to compress, and these photos are labelled.
tasks.q: A factory has thousands of photos from its production line, each labelled defective or not, and wants a network that flags the defective ones. Which type of network fits?
options: A feedforward network, fed each photo flattened into one long row.
A convolutional network, which slides the same detector over the photo.
A recurrent network such as an LSTM, which carries a memory forward.
An autoencoder, which squeezes each photo through a narrow middle layer.
tasks.explain: Ask what one input looks like: here it is an image, and a convolutional network reads grid data by reusing the same small detector at every position, so neighbouring pixels stay together. Flattening the photo for a feedforward network loses the fact that two pixels were neighbours.

tasks.title: A dense layer
tasks.idea: The reader writes dense_relu(x, W, b) in plain Python: x is a list of inputs, W a list of rows with shape (inputs, units), b a list of one bias per unit, and it returns a list with one value per unit, max(0, weighted sum + bias). With x = [2.0, 1.0, 3.0], W = [[0.5], [-1.0], [0.25]] and b = [0.5] it returns [1.25].
checks: Returns [1.25] for the page's one-neuron example; leaving out the bias gives [0.75].
A unit whose weighted sum plus bias is negative comes back as 0.0; skipping ReLU returns the negative value.
With two inputs and three units it returns three values, unit j using column j of W; reading W as (units, inputs), the shape the page warns about, gives the wrong numbers or an IndexError.
tasks.q: Write dense_relu(x, W, b), one dense layer followed by ReLU, with plain Python lists instead of numpy. x is a list of inputs. W is a list of rows with the shape (inputs, units), so it has one row per input and column j holds the weights of unit j. b holds one bias per unit. Return a list with one value per unit: that unit's weighted sum of the inputs, plus its bias, through ReLU, max(0, ...). For example, dense_relu([2.0, 1.0, 3.0], [[0.5], [-1.0], [0.25]], [0.5]) returns [1.25], the page's one neuron.
tasks.tests:
assert dense_relu([2.0, 1.0, 3.0], [[0.5], [-1.0], [0.25]], [0.5]) == [1.25], "the page's one neuron adds its bias to the weighted sum"
assert dense_relu([1.0, 2.0], [[1.0], [-1.0]], [0.5]) == [0.0], "a unit whose weighted sum plus bias is negative comes back as 0.0"
assert dense_relu([1.0, 2.0], [[1.0, 0.5, -1.0], [2.0, 0.25, 3.0]], [0.0, 1.0, -2.0]) == [5.0, 2.0, 3.0], "two inputs and three units give three values, unit j using column j of W"

tasks.title: Sliding a kernel
tasks.idea: The reader writes correlate_valid(image, kernel) in plain Python with lists of lists: it slides the kernel unflipped over every position where it fits, multiplies and sums, and returns the feature map. On a 4 by 4 grid that is dark (0) in its left two columns and bright (9) in its right two, the vertical-edge kernel [[-1, 0, 1]] * 3 gives [[27, 27], [27, 27]].
checks: The 4 by 4 edge image with the page's vertical-edge kernel gives a 2 by 2 result, n - k + 1 on each side; looping over every pixel gives the wrong size or an IndexError.
That dark-to-bright edge scores +27 at every position; flipping the kernel first, as convolve2d does, scores -27.
A non-symmetric kernel on a small grid gives the sum of all nine products at each position; summing only one row or column of the patch gives a different map.
tasks.q: Write correlate_valid(image, kernel) with plain Python lists of rows, as correlate2d(image, kernel, mode="valid") computes it. Slide the kernel over the image without flipping it, visiting only the positions where the whole kernel fits. At each position multiply every pixel by the weight on top of it and add all the products. Return the feature map as a list of rows: a k by k kernel on an n by n image gives n - k + 1 rows of n - k + 1 values. For example, on the page's 4 by 4 image, every row [0, 0, 9, 9], the vertical-edge kernel [[-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1]] gives [[27, 27], [27, 27]].
tasks.tests:
edge = [[0, 0, 9, 9], [0, 0, 9, 9], [0, 0, 9, 9], [0, 0, 9, 9]]
vertical = [[-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1]]
grid = [[1, 2, 0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 2, 3, 1], [2, 0, 1, 1, 0], [1, 3, 0, 2, 2], [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]]
kernel = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 0], [-1, 0, 3]]
assert [len(row) for row in correlate_valid(edge, vertical)] == [2, 2], "a 3 by 3 kernel on a 4 by 4 image gives 2 rows of 2, n - k + 1 on each side"
assert correlate_valid(edge, vertical) == [[27, 27], [27, 27]], "the dark-to-bright edge scores +27 with the kernel unflipped"
assert correlate_valid(grid, kernel) == [[3, 9, 8], [3, 11, 11], [10, 1, 5]], "each value is the sum of all nine products of a patch and the kernel"

tasks.title: Image classification
tasks.idea: Three image jobs are on offer, and the question asks which one most needs a CNN instead of a flat classifier on pixels. The right pick is large product photos where the defect can sit anywhere in the frame, since the flat model's first layer would need millions of weights and shifted objects confuse it.
checks: Picking the 8 by 8 centred digits catches the belief that a CNN always pays off on images; the page says the flat baseline already scores 96 percent there.
Picking a small table of form fields catches confusing deep learning in general with a CNN; the page says a CNN reads grid data and small tables suit classical models.
tasks.q: Three classification jobs could each start with a flat classifier fed the raw values, the way the page's baseline reads digit pixels. Which job most needs a convolutional network instead?
options: Large product photos where a defect can sit anywhere in the frame.
Handwritten digits of 8 by 8 pixels, each one centred in its grid.
A small table of application-form fields such as income and age.
tasks.explain: On a large photo the flat model's first layer needs millions of weights, each tied to one pixel position, so a defect that moves around the frame confuses it, while a CNN reuses a few kernel weights at every position. On 64-pixel centred digits the flat baseline already scores 96 percent.

tasks.title: Bag of words
tasks.idea: The reader writes bag_of_words(text, vocabulary) in plain Python: it lowercases the text, splits it on spaces, and returns a list with one count per vocabulary word, in the vocabulary's order. With vocabulary ["blocked", "login", "refund", "works"], the title "Refund blocked login works" returns [1, 1, 1, 1].
checks: "Login page Login" over a vocabulary holding login and page returns 2 under login; leaving out the lowercasing counts only one, or none.
A title with a word missing from the vocabulary returns a row the length of the vocabulary, the unseen word dropped; appending a column for it or raising a KeyError fails.
"Refund blocked login works" and "Login blocked refund works" return the same row; counting by position in the title instead of by vocabulary word gives different rows.
tasks.q: Write bag_of_words(text, vocabulary) in plain Python. Lowercase text and split it on spaces into tokens. Return a list with one count per word of vocabulary, in the vocabulary's order: how many tokens are that word. A token that is not in the vocabulary is dropped, the way a fitted vectorizer drops a word it never saw. For example, bag_of_words("Refund blocked login works", ["blocked", "login", "refund", "works"]) returns [1, 1, 1, 1].
tasks.tests:
vocab = ["blocked", "login", "refund", "works"]
assert bag_of_words("Login page Login", ["login", "page"]) == [2, 1], "a word repeated in another case is counted every time"
assert bag_of_words("Refund invoice blocked", vocab) == [1, 0, 1, 0], "a word missing from the vocabulary is dropped, one count per vocabulary word"
assert bag_of_words("Login blocked refund works", vocab) == [1, 1, 1, 1], "the same words in another order give the same row"

tasks.title: The text pipeline
tasks.idea: A teammate has a fitted make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(...), LogisticRegression(...)) router and wants a label for one new ticket title. The right pick is clf.predict([title]), which sends the title through transform with the training vocabulary before the model sees it.
checks: Calling fit_transform on the new title before predicting catches the brief's pitfall; the page says it builds a fresh vocabulary from that one title, so the columns no longer match the model's.

Passing the raw title straight to the LogisticRegression step catches skipping the vectorizer; the page says every model needs numbers and the components run tokenizer, vocabulary, vectorizer, model, in that order.

Refitting the vectorizer on the training titles plus the new one so its unseen words get columns catches misreading where the vocabulary comes from; the page says it is learned from training text only and unseen words are ignored.
tasks.q: A teammate has fitted clf = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)) on the training ticket titles and wants a label for one new title, held in title. What should they do?
options: Run fit_transform on the new title, then predict from that row.
Pass the raw title straight to the LogisticRegression step.
Refit the vectorizer on the training titles plus the new one, then predict.
Call clf.predict([title]) on the fitted pipeline as it stands.
tasks.explain: The pipeline's predict sends the title through transform, which reuses the vocabulary learned from the training text, before the model sees it, and any word it never saw is ignored. fit_transform would build a fresh vocabulary from the new title alone, so the columns no longer match the model's.
